newsitem.title: USA: Bergen CFO sees $30 mln annual cost savings.
newsitem.headline: Bergen CFO sees $30 mln annual cost savings.

text.p: Bergen Brunswig Corp Chief Financial Officer Neil Dimick said he expects $30 million in annual cost savings from his company's $3.2 billion merger with generic drug maker IVAX Corp.
He said he expects the merger to be slightly dilutive in 1997 but to become accretive in 1998.

BBI Healthcare Corp, the new company to be formed in the merger, would probably not match Wall Street expectations for 1997 earnings of $2.10 a share, which analysts have been predicting for Bergen Brunswig, he said.
"The deal should be slightly dilutive in the first six to eight months of 1997, and then we should start to grow at about 25 percent annually," Dimick said late Monday at a gathering for reporters.
"In 1998, I think we're looking at earnings growth in the mid-20's, accretive over where we would have been without the merger."
BBI is to acquire Bergen Brunswig and IVAX in stock swaps, exchanging one BBI share for each Bergen Brunswig share, and 0.42 BBI share for each IVAX share, the companies said on Monday.
Executives of the two companies expressed surprise after their stocks dropped sharply on Monday following the merger announcement.
"We thought we'd be down about a buck or so," Dimick said.

Shares of Bergen Brunswig fell 5-1/8 to 27-5/8 and IVAX shares fell 3-3/8 to 12-3/8 as investers fretted over whether some drug suppliers would be less willing to do business with Bergen Brunswig once it had a lower-cost in-house supplier of generic drugs.

Robert Martini, chairman and chief executive of Bergen Brunswig, said that although he expects some suppliers to try other sources, BBI's ability to compete with low-cost generic drugs means the company will not lose many customers.
Bergen Brunswig officials also said the stock fall may have been caused by uncertainty on the part of Wall Street investors about the merger, since it is a vertical integration.

IVAX posted a third quarter loss of $1.47 a share, compared to a profit of $0.23 last year. The loss included a $104.3 million pre-tax charge relating to the write-down of goodwill and certain fixed assets of its U.S. generic drug distribution business and certain product lines of its specialty chemicals business, and $14 million of other charges.
IVAX shares have been beseiged by inventory and customer credit problems for the past two quarters. Its stock price has fallen sharply from around 23-3/4 in late June.

The $104.3 million charge should help control inventory problems in the short-term, said Bergen Brunswig President and Chief Executive Officer-elect Donald Roden. He said the due diligence process "might have contributed" to IVAX's decision to take the balance sheet reserve item.
In the long-term, Roden said he expects Bergen Brunswig's strong inventory controls to correct the problems.
Martini and IVAX Chairmen Phillip Frost said the companies had been in discussions about a merger for just over two years. Frost said IVAX had not been in talks to merge with any other companies.

Frost said he expects further consolidation among generic-durg manufacturers. "There's going to be a shake-out. The mergers are more likely to be horizontal, but it would mean less cut-throat price cutting as well as more stability and profitability among those who do survive," he said.
Frost owns about 16 percent of IVAX, and Martini owns about 7.0 percent of Bergen Brunswig, Dimick said. Both men have agreed to vote their shares in favor of the merger.
The companies did disclose details about future profit margins.
-- Jennifer Westhoven, Wall Street Desk (212) 859-1730
